data: HEO-segment IR early warning — covers polar latitudes the GEO sensors can't

SBIRS HEO-1 launched 2006-06-28 as a hosted payload on USA-184. The HEO-segment infrared sensors dwell at apogee over the polar regions to detect missile launches from latitudes where the geostationary DSP / SBIRS-GEO sensors look at too low an angle. Successor to the DSP early-warning constellation.
US early-warning IR sensors hosted on classified Tundra-orbit platforms

The HEO segment of the US Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) — infrared missile-warning sensors hosted on classified host satellites in the 24-hour Tundra orbit at the 63.4° critical inclination. By dwelling at apogee over high latitudes, SBIRS-HEO covers the polar regions where geostationary DSP / SBIRS-GEO sensors look at too low an angle. SBIRS HEO-1 launched in 2006 as a hosted payload on USA-184.
The original GNSS — 31 satellites, free public service since 2000
Europe's civilian GNSS — ~30 sats, sub-metre positioning
China's GNSS — global ops since 2020; unique MEO + IGSO + GEO hybrid
Only operational MEO commercial broadband — 20+ sats

High-eccentricity orbits at 63.4° critical inclination. Molniya (12-hour, 600 × 40,000 km) — Russian high-latitude comms + Oko/Meridian early warning since 1965. Tundra (24-hour, ~25,000 × ~47,000 km) — Sirius XM Satellite Radio + US SBIRS-HEO sensors.
